prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators are the broadest point of agreement in the room: seven of eight members ranked B012, four of them in the top three, and all seven proposed the same trio. The discovery is concrete (a new classification of band insulators with protected edge states, predicted by Kane and Mele and observed in HgTe quantum wells by Molenkamp's group), it has been confirmed for more than fifteen years across transport, ARPES and STM, and its interpretation is stable. It is a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing that fits the discovery criterion without the interpretive caveats that still hang over the newer moire work. Having put the gamma-ray burst afterglow case (B031) first in my opening ballot, I have to be honest that it drew no other support; I do not think a candidate with a single advocate, and one whose field is close to my own, should drive the committee's configuration, so I am moving to the candidate that most colleagues can defend on the merits.
statement.case_against: The credited trio is incomplete. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional topological-insulator work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hsieh and Hasan is separate and is also omitted. The 2016 prize on topological phases of matter also raises a fair question about whether the committee is returning too quickly to a closely related area. If the committee judges that the attribution cannot be fairly drawn with three names, the case weakens substantially.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clear prediction followed by an experimental discovery, reproduced in many labs and reshaping a field, while calling the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity still debated.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 experiments are a compelling pair and I ranked B047 third myself. Where I differ is on maturity. Reproducibility of the phenomenology is not in dispute, but the nature of the superconducting and correlated phases is, and the committee would be crediting a discovery whose physical meaning is still being argued. About seven years is also short next to the fifteen-plus years of stable interpretation behind B012. I keep B047 as my first alternative and would support it if the committee judges the discovery separately from its explanation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B012 fourth, calling Z2 a distinct and fundamental advance but slightly overshadowed by the 2016 prize on topological phases, and notes the credited list is defensible but incomplete. He also judges B047 probably early for a prize.
responses.response: I share both qualifications and they are why I treat B012 as the preferred option and not an unqualified one. The 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall-type topological phases. The Z2 invariant and time-reversal-protected edge states are a separate discovery that came later, with its own experimental verification. On attribution I agree the trio is incomplete, but Kane and Mele made the foundational proposal and Molenkamp the first observation, and I do not see a cleaner three-name split anywhere in this topic. Your doubt about B047 being early is my own reason for ranking it below B012. I would add that your first choice, dynamical mean-field theory (B005), is a strong methodological case, but it drew four rankings in total and does not match the breadth of support behind B012.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, as an original idea by Katori realised by Ye at the 10^-18 level with no competing claim to the core concept. She ranks B012 second, with credit shared with Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator authors.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of B019 as the cleanest attribution on the table, and I ranked it fifth. I find it hard to rank it above the topological-insulator work because it has the narrowest scientific footprint of the leading candidates, and the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling quantum systems already sit near it. It would be a respectable prize but not clearly the most consequential. On B012 you identify the same attribution problem I do. I would argue that the Nobel record contains many cases where the prize went to the decisive prediction and the first observation and left the wider community out, and Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are the clearest such trio here.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B019 first, arguing that the lattice clock is a concrete advance in measurement accuracy that opens relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants, with a timely and arguably overdue redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I take the instrument-driven argument seriously, since I value precision measurement. The case is strong, and Katori and Ye are an unusually clean pair. My reservation is the definition of the second: the redefinition is still a prospect, and the geodesy and constants applications are still being demonstrated, so the prize would reward capability more than a completed discovery. I would not object strongly to B019 and have listed it as an alternative, but I would not make it the lead while B012 has more support and a long record of confirmation. I would also like to hear whether you see the pending redefinition as a reason to wait or to act now.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active-matter hydrodynamics (Vicsek, Toner, Tu and Ramaswamy) first as having established active matter as a coherent branch of nonequilibrium statistical physics, with long-range order in two dimensions and giant number fluctuations, and a stable theory over about three decades.
responses.response: The conceptual originality is real, and the order in two dimensions that violates the Mermin-Wagner expectation is a striking result. My difficulty is in the credit and the evidence. Tu, a co-author of the continuum theory, is not on the credited list, and the quantitative tests of the Toner-Tu exponents in clean experiments are limited compared with how thoroughly the quantum spin Hall edge states have been tested. I also note that no other member ranked B009 within the shortlist support, so as chair I would want the committee to hear the case in detail before this candidate is judged. I have not placed it in my configuration or alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a fair attribution given the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the separate 3D topological-insulator contributors.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases makes a return to topological matter premature for the committee.
Whether the physical interpretation of magic-angle graphene will settle quickly enough to move B047 ahead of B012.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should count as maturity for B019 or as a reason to wait.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate on the shortlist matches a documented personal or institutional tie in my profile. The gamma-ray burst afterglow candidate (B031) that I ranked first lies close to my gamma-ray and hard-X-ray instrumentation work (Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur), so I flag that field-adjacent connection and have not included B031 in my configuration or alternatives. No specific conflict is apparent for B012, B047 or B019.
